extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, poets, and critics interested in epic poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the 'sentiments' (thoughts, speech, and behaviour) and related qualities in epic poetry, using Aristotle's framework and examples from Homer, Virgil, and Milton. Emphasises what sentiments should be, what to avoid, and how they contribute to an epic's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-part critical framework (fable, characters, sentiments, language)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete critical consideration of an epic poem should survey the Fable (plot), the Characters (manners), the Sentiments (thoughts/speech), and the Language (diction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author follows Aristotle's arrangement: having surveyed fable and characters, he now treats Sentiments and Language. This structural division indicates a rubric for comprehensive criticism: treat each head in turn and give particular instances of beauties and blemishes under each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of Sentiments (conformity to character and subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments are just when they are conformable to the characters of the several persons and adapted to the Subject (Things) introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the thoughts and behaviours ascribed to persons fit their established character and whether the sentiments relate properly to the subject-matter. If sentiments misfit a character or subject, they are unjust. (Text explicitly: 'Sentiments ... are just when they are conformable to the characters of the several Persons' and 'are then perfect when they are such as are adapted to the Subject.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments should serve intended emotional ends
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet uses sentiments to argue, explain, magnify, diminish, or to raise particular passions (love, hatred, pity, terror, etc.), the sentiments must be proper for those ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should assess whether a given passage's thoughts are fitted to produce the targeted emotion or rhetorical effect. The same sentiment may be appropriate or inappropriate depending on the intended passion or argumentative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor natural and sublime thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should abound with two kinds of sentiments: the natural (appropriate to human nature) and the sublime (grand, elevating thoughts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity is a chief excellence in epic writing; Milton is praised for the greatness of his sentiments, especially in certain books (1,2,6,7). Compare poets: Virgil has fewer sublime thoughts than Homer; Milton rivals Homer in sublimity. Aim both for naturalness and the capacity to elevate the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity as distinguishing epic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatness or sublimity of thoughts is a distinguishing excellence of an epic poem and a mark of superior genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge an epic by its capacity to present large, transporting ideas (the author cites Milton's first, second, sixth and seventh books as examples). Use parallels from Longinus and examples from Homer to measure sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected and unnatural sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not employ affected, unnatural, or overly refined thoughts — these are defects in epic sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should identify points of false refinement or artificiality (common in later ages) and attribute some historical or cultural origins where appropriate. Examples of such faults are ascribed to later poets (Ovid, Statins, Claudian, Tasso) rather than to Homer or Virgil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean and vulgar sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should not include mean, groveling, or vulgar thoughts that lower the tone; such sentiments are improper because an epic's business is to excite noble passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiments that provoke laughter or triviality are generally unsuitable in heroic/epic poetry except where deliberately and properly timed. Homer has some homeliness attributable to his age; Virgil rarely lapses into meanness; Milton has very few such blemishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone consistency: avoid burlesque or unsuitable mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic tone should remain largely serious; burlesque, puns, or trivial scoffing are objectionable unless they occur in moments where the reader's disposition allows relaxation (well-timed comic relief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author singles out a passage in Paradise Lost (the satanic scoffing/puns about dancing and composition) as the poem's most exceptionable passage. By contrast, a single laugh in the Aeneid (Book V) is acceptable because it is well timed in a book of games and diversions. Assess whether moments of levity are fitting in context and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive characters require especially apt sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet invents characters 'out of nature' (e.g., Adam and Eve before the Fall, Milton's infernal council), it is more challenging and praiseworthy to supply proper sentiments for them than for characters drawn from known history or common life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how well the poet creates and sustains appropriate speech and behaviour for wholly invented beings: success here indicates higher genius. The critic should note the difficulty and reward of furnishing such characters with befitting sentiments and give credit when accomplished (Milton praised for this).
